actions.oldValue: A revenge tragedy centered on a Roman general whose victory ignites a cycle of brutality. What begins as a triumph of state power descends into escalating violence, exposing how vengeance corrodes personal, political, and moral order. actions.oldValue: A comic, insightful look at Deaf identity, co-written by James Caverly and Andrew Morrill. Tim and Jake are Deaf roommates living in a city apartment—but that’s about all they have in common. While one embraces Deaf culture with pride and resistance, the other seeks to navigate the hearing world with different priorities. As they clash over everyday tasks—like taking out the trash—their disagreement grows into a sharply comic, layered exploration of identity, communication, and what it really means to understand someone else’s experience. The play is co-written by James Caverly (known for Only Murders in the Building) and Andrew Morrill, both of whom bring personal insight and authenticity to the characters and their world. With a libretto by renowned author Sofi Oksanen, the opera unfolds through a hauntingly beautiful soundscape that blends traditional opera, expressionistic speak-singing, and Scandinavian folk music. Set a decade after the tragedy, the story follows a young couple whose wedding unexpectedly reopens old wounds, revealing long-buried secrets. actions.newValue: A musical exploring inherited trauma, activism, and the legacy of the Greensboro Massacre. It follows a narrative shaped by the aftermath of that violence, tracing how its impact extends across generations. What begins as an attempt to document history evolves into a broader exploration of memory, trauma, and the lingering presence of unresolved events. Created by César James Alvarez, who was born into the survivor community, the musical shifts between personal reflection and collective experience.

actions.oldValue: A Scottish nobleman and his wife descend into violence after seizing the throne. Based on William Shakespeare’s tragedy, Macbeth follows the rise and collapse of a Scottish nobleman driven by prophecy and political ambition. Urged on by Lady Macbeth, Macbeth murders King Duncan to seize the throne, setting off a cycle of paranoia, violence, and guilt that consumes both husband and wife. Giuseppe Verdi’s opera adaptation emphasizes the psychological unraveling of the central couple through large-scale choral scenes and dramatic vocal writing. This new production at The Metropolitan Opera is directed by Louisa Proske, whose recent international opera and theatre productions have drawn attention for contemporary reinterpretations of classic works. actions.oldValue: Two teens at a Christian summer camp confront faith, desire, and identity. Forced to share a room at a conservative Christian summer camp, Ryan and Jabez begin the week expecting conflict rather than connection. Ryan appears composed and devout, while Jabez resists the camp’s rigid expectations with open cynicism. actions.oldValue: A governess risks scandal after rebelling against the life imposed on her. Written by Cicely Hamilton in 1911, PHYL follows Phyllis Chester, a governess trapped in an isolated and restrictive existence. Frustrated by the limitations placed on her life and desires, she acts impulsively in a way that threatens her social standing and future. The play examines questions of female independence, sexuality, and respectability within the constraints of early 20th-century society. Originally banned from performance at Oxford University despite passing official censorship without required edits, the play instead premiered in Manchester, where contemporary critics reacted strongly to its treatment of women’s desire and personal freedom. actions.newValue: Rosie O’Donnell delivers a solo stage memoir blending comedy and personal storytelling. Rosie O’Donnell returns to the stage with a solo performance shaped by reflections on her career, personal life, and recent experiences living abroad. The piece follows her journey through identity, motherhood, cultural transition, and the shifting landscape of her life after decades in entertainment. Written and performed by Rosie O’Donnell (A League of Their Own, Sleepless in Seattle, The Rosie O’Donnell Show) and directed by Gabriel Barre (Amazing Grace, Chaplin), the production draws on O’Donnell’s extensive career across film, television, and theatre. It marks her first new stage show in nearly a decade, presented following international engagements in Dublin, Edinburgh, and Australia.
